groups.instructions: Complete the flow-chart below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.strategy: Flow-charts describe a process or sequence in order. Follow the arrows and keep track of where you are in the passage.

questions.prompt: Location of the experiment: a ________ supermarket.
questions.explanation: 'a Californian supermarket'. Copy the word exactly as it appears — you may not change 'Californian' into 'California'.

questions.prompt: A stand offered either six or ________ kinds of jam.
The larger display caused more people to stop and ________.
questions.explanation: 'attracted more passers-by to stop and taste'.

questions.prompt: Result: about ________ of people who saw the small display bought jam.
questions.explanation: 'around 30 per cent of shoppers who had seen the small selection'.

questions.prompt: Conclusion: too many options can reduce people's ________ to choose.
questions.explanation: 'could reduce people's motivation to choose at all'.

groups.instructions: Classify the following statements as referring to A — maximisers, B — satisficers, C — both maximisers and satisficers.

questions.prompt: They choose the first option that is good enough.
questions.explanation: 'satisficers … are content to select the first option that meets their requirements'.

questions.prompt: They tend to achieve better results in objective terms.
They are more satisfied with their decisions.
questions.explanation: Maximisers 'report feeling less satisfied … than satisficers do'.

questions.prompt: They feel the need to consider every alternative.
questions.explanation: Maximisers 'feel they must examine every possibility'.

groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.prompt: What did the statistical review find?

options.text: The original jam study had been carried out incorrectly.
On average across studies, choice overload had almost no effect.
Choice overload is stronger in supermarkets than elsewhere.

questions.explanation: 'the average effect of choice overload across all of them was close to zero'.
questions.trap: A — the writer says 'This does not necessarily mean the original finding was wrong.'

questions.prompt: Which condition makes choice overload MORE likely?

options.text: the chooser already knows what they want
the options are grouped into categories
there is little time to decide

questions.explanation: 'when the choice must be made quickly'. A, B and D all reduce overload.

questions.prompt: The writer mentions a wine enthusiast and a novice to show that

options.text: experts make better decisions than beginners.
the same choice can affect people differently.
shops should stock fewer types of wine.

questions.explanation: One 'may enjoy the variety'; the other 'may find the same shelf paralysing'.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's overall view?

options.text: Classical economists were right about choice.
Offering fewer options is the best policy.
The presentation of choices matters as much as their number.

questions.explanation: Final paragraph: 'the question is not simply "how many options?" but "how can people be helped to navigate them?"'
